name: Manny Machado
description: Manny Machado, born 6 July 1992 in Miami, Florida, is a Dominican-American third baseman for the San Diego Padres and one of the most durable stars of his generation. The son of Dominican parents Manuel and Rosa Machado, he was drafted third overall by the Baltimore Orioles in 2010 and debuted on 9 August 2012. He won Gold Glove Awards in 2013 and 2015, was traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers in 2018, and signed with San Diego in 2019, later extending on an 11-year contract that runs through 2033. A seven-time All-Star and three-time Silver Slugger, he reached 2,000 career hits on 7 July 2025, becoming the fifth active player to the mark. Machado has represented the Dominican Republic at the World Baseball Classic in 2017, 2023 and 2026, publicly grounding that choice in his Dominican parentage. Through the 2026 season he had 2,197 hits, 399 home runs and 1,235 RBIs, and he led the 2026 Padres with 30 home runs and 91 RBIs.

name: Marian Anderson
description: Marian Anderson (1897–1993), the Philadelphia-born contralto, possessed what conductor Arturo Toscanini called a voice heard once in a hundred years. Raised in South Philadelphia and formed in her church choir, she was denied admission to a white music academy because of her race and built her technique through community-funded lessons; her first great triumphs came on European stages. Returning home acclaimed, she still met Jim Crow at every turn — segregated trains, whites-only audiences, hotels that would not house her. In 1939 the Daughters of the American Revolution refused her Washington's Constitution Hall. Eleanor Roosevelt resigned her DAR membership in protest, and on Easter Sunday, April 9, 1939, Anderson sang from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial before some 75,000 people and a radio audience of millions — a defining early moment of the civil rights movement, which Howard University had set in motion by seeking the hall for her concert. The DAR reversed course and hosted her in 1943; in 1955 she became the first Black singer to perform a leading role at the Metropolitan Opera. She sang at two presidential inaugurations, returned to the Memorial for the 1963 March on Washington, and retired after a 1964–65 farewell tour.

name: Margzetta Frazier
description: Margzetta Bryantina Frazier, born 25 February 2000 in Pennsylvania and raised in Sicklerville, New Jersey, is an American artistic gymnast. Trained at the Parkettes National Training Center in Allentown, she represented the United States in 2017 and 2018 and won the all-around silver medal at the 2018 Birmingham World Cup. At UCLA, where she competed from 2019 to 2024, she became a four-time All-American and the 2021 Pac-12 uneven bars champion and helped the Bruins to the NCAA team bronze in 2019. Her February 2021 floor routine set to Janet Jackson's music went viral. A sociology graduate who completed a postgraduate certificate in project management in 2024, Frazier co-founded UCLA's Black Student-Athlete Alliance, and her official UCLA biography lists Dominique Dawes among the athletes she admires. She retired from competition in March 2024 after six UCLA seasons and now works as a poet, singer and creator. Her younger sister eMjae is also an elite gymnast, at California.

name: Mike Epps
description: Mike Epps, born Michael Elliot Epps on 18 November 1970 in Indianapolis, Indiana, is an American stand-up comedian and actor. Raised on Indianapolis's east side, he left for New York in 1994 and broke nationally on HBO's Def Comedy Jam in 1995, later hosting the show. His film breakthrough came as Day-Day Jones in Next Friday (2000) and Friday After Next (2002) opposite Ice Cube, and he reached a wider audience as 'Black Doug' in The Hangover (2009) and in the Resident Evil films. He has also taken dramatic turns — playing Richard Pryor in Nina (2016) and appearing in Sparkle and Dolemite Is My Name — and won NAACP Image Awards for Jumping the Broom (2011) and Survivor's Remorse (2016). Since 2021 he has co-created and starred in the Indianapolis-set Netflix sitcom The Upshaws, and his 2018 memoir Unsuccessful Thug recounts the Indianapolis childhood behind the act. He continues to headline arena tours in 2026.

name: Myrtis Dightman
aliases: Myrtis Dightman Sr.; Myrtis Dee Dightman; Jackie Robinson of Rodeo (nickname); Jackie Robinson of Professional Rodeo (nickname)
description: Myrtis Dightman, born May 7, 1935, in Crockett, Texas, and raised on a ranch where his father worked, is a pioneering Black professional bull rider often called the Jackie Robinson of rodeo. He began in rodeo as a bullfighter, earned his Professional Rodeo Cowboys Association card in 1957, and in 1964 became the first Black cowboy to qualify for the National Finals Rodeo. He qualified seven times in all, finishing third in the world standings in 1967 and again in 1968, and won major events including the Calgary Stampede and Cheyenne Frontier Days. He mentored Charlie Sampson, who in 1982 became the first Black bull rider to win a world championship. Dightman was inducted into the ProRodeo Hall of Fame in 2016 and the PBR Ring of Honor in 2003, and a bronze statue stands at the Porth Agricultural Arena in Crockett, where an annual Labor Day rodeo bears his name. In May 2025 the National Cowboy Museum reported that he still lived in Houston and was celebrating his ninetieth birthday.

name: Michael W. Twitty
description: Michael W. Twitty is an African American Jewish writer, culinary historian, historical interpreter, and educator born in Washington, D.C., in 1977. He first became interested in traditional cooking as a child on a trip to Colonial Williamsburg, and he majored in African American studies and anthropology at Howard University without finishing because of financial constraints. In 2010 he launched Afroculinaria, a culinary history blog covering African and African American foodways, described by the Miami Book Fair as the first blog devoted to African American historic foodways and their legacies. His book The Cooking Gene, published by HarperCollins/Amistad, traces his African American ancestry through food from Africa to America and examines the origins of soul food, barbecue, and Southern cuisine. It won the 2018 James Beard Foundation Book Award for Book of the Year as well as the category for writing. The University of Washington Magazine identifies him as the first Black author to garner the James Beard Award for Writing. His later books include Koshersoul, published in 2022, exploring African and Jewish diaspora cuisines, and Recipes From the American South, published by Phaidon in 2025.

name: Michelle Duster
description: Michelle Duster is a Chicago-born author, professor, public historian, and champion of racial and gender equity. The HistoryMakers biography states she was born in Chicago, Illinois, on December 20, 1963, earned a B.A. in psychology from Dartmouth College in 1985, and earned an M.A. in media studies from The New School in 1997. She is the great-granddaughter of journalist and activist Ida B. Wells. Duster edited two anthologies of Wells's writing, Ida in Her Own Words in 2008 and Ida From Abroad in 2010, and in 2008 she joined the Ida B. Wells Commemorative Art Committee, which commissioned the Ida B. Wells National Monument. In 2015 she became an adjunct professor at Columbia College Chicago. Her biography Ida B. the Queen: The Extraordinary Life and Legacy of Ida B. Wells was published on January 26, 2021, by Simon & Schuster, followed by the children's book Ida B. Wells, Voice of Truth in 2022. That same year she spoke at the White House for the signing of the Emmett Till Anti-Lynching Act, and she resides in Chicago.

name: Mississippi Goddam
description: "Mississippi Goddam" is a song written and performed by American singer and pianist Nina Simone, who later called it her first civil rights song. Released in 1964 on her album Nina Simone in Concert, drawn from recordings of three Carnegie Hall concerts earlier that year, the song was her first release for the Dutch label Philips Records and marked a more political turn in her recorded music. Simone composed it in less than an hour. The song captures her response to the racially motivated murders of Emmett Till and Medgar Evers in Mississippi and to the 16th Street Baptist Church bombing in Birmingham, Alabama, which killed four Black children. She first performed it at the Village Gate nightclub in Greenwich Village, and shortly afterward in March 1964 at Carnegie Hall before a mostly white audience. The Carnegie Hall recording was released as a single and became an anthem of the Civil Rights Movement, while the song was banned in several Southern states and promotional singles were returned broken in half. In 2019 the Library of Congress selected it for the National Recording Registry.

name: Marlon Wayans
description: Marlon Lamont Wayans is an American actor, comedian, writer, and producer born on July 23, 1972, in New York City. He is the youngest of ten siblings in the Wayans family, raised in the Fulton Houses housing project in New York City, and he attended Fiorello H. LaGuardia High School of Music & Art and Performing Arts before attending Howard University, which he left after two years. He appeared with his siblings on the sketch comedy show In Living Color between 1992 and 1993, and from 1995 to 1999 he co-starred with his brother Shawn Wayans in the WB sitcom The Wayans Bros. With Shawn he is best known for the comedy films Don't Be a Menace, Scary Movie and Scary Movie 2, White Chicks, and Little Man, producing the first two Scary Movie films, in which the brothers were credited writers and co-stars. He also earned critical attention for a dramatic role in Requiem for a Dream in 2000, starred in the NBC sitcom Marlon in 2017 and 2018, played Ted White in Respect in 2021, and starred in the horror film Him in 2025.

name: Ma Rainey
aliases: Gertrude "Ma" Rainey; Gertrude Pridgett; Madame Rainey
description: Gertrude "Ma" Rainey, born Gertrude Pridgett on April 26, 1886, in Columbus, Georgia — a birth year and place some researchers dispute — was an American blues singer billed as the "Mother of the Blues". She began performing as a teenager, married William "Pa" Rainey in 1904, and toured with the Rabbit Foot Minstrels before the pair billed themselves as Rainey and Rainey, Assassinators of the Blues. The New Georgia Encyclopedia credits her with helping establish classic blues as a staple of American musical life and with linking country blues to the urban blues of the 1920s. Signing with Paramount Records, she made her first recordings in December 1923 and produced more than 100 recordings over five years, including "Bo-Weevil Blues", "Moonshine Blues" and "Ma Rainey's Black Bottom" (1927), accompanied at times by Louis Armstrong and her own Georgia Jazz Band. From 1924 she toured the Theater Owners Booking Association circuit in the South and Midwest. Paramount dropped her in 1928; she later retired to Georgia, where she ran theatres, and died on December 22, 1939. She entered the Blues Hall of Fame in 1983 and the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 1990.

name: Maggie Lena Walker
aliases: Maggie L. Walker; Maggie Lena Draper; Maggie Lena Mitchell
description: Maggie Lena Walker (July 15, 1864 – December 15, 1934) was a Richmond, Virginia, businesswoman, teacher and civic leader. Born Maggie Lena Draper, the daughter of a formerly enslaved mother who worked as a laundress, she joined the Independent Order of St. Luke as a teenager and rose to its top leadership post, Right Worthy Grand Secretary, in 1899, reviving the struggling mutual-aid society. In 1902 she founded its newspaper, the St. Luke Herald. In November 1903 she chartered the St. Luke Penny Savings Bank in Richmond and served as its first president — recognized by the National Park Service and the Library of Congress as the first African American woman to charter a bank in the United States, and described in the Park Service's historic-site summary as the first woman in the country to charter and serve as president of a bank. The bank employed mainly African American women and made many mortgage loans in Richmond's Black community. Walker oversaw its merger with two other Black-owned banks into the Consolidated Bank and Trust Company, serving as board chair until her death. Her Jackson Ward home is the Maggie L. Walker National Historic Site.

name: Mya Nicole
description: Mya Nicole Johnson, born 20 December 2005 in Houston, Texas, is an American TikTok creator, dancer and actress known as Mya Nicole. An African-American creator and a member of the social media group Tha Bad Kids, she built her following on dance videos posted to TikTok and Instagram under the handle @theemyanicole, after starting out on Dubsmash. In February 2021 she and fellow creator Chris Cotter created the viral dance to Cardi B's "Up." When Addison Rae performed the dance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon without on-screen credit to its creators, the segment drew wide criticism, and Fallon then invited Johnson and Cotter onto the show to perform their own choreography. Johnson released her own song, "You Ain't Like That," featuring Rakihya Raine, in November 2021, and in 2022 she played Lisa in the third season of Brat TV's Crown Lake.

name: Motsi Mabuse
description: Motshegetsi Mabuse, known as Motsi Mabuse, born 11 April 1981 in Mankwe, South Africa, is a South African dancer based in Germany. Her family moved to Pretoria when she was five, and she and her younger sister Oti both took up dancing there. Expected to become a lawyer, she studied at the University of Pretoria before dance took over; she was runner-up in the South African national championships in 1998 and met her first dance partner, Timo Kulczak, at the British Open Championships in Blackpool in 1999. Competing internationally from Germany, she became a German Latin champion and, in 2013, won the German Latin dance contest with Ukrainian dancer Evgenij Voznyuk, whom she later married. She appeared on Germany's Let's Dance first as a professional dancer and has been a judge on that show since 2011. In 2019 she joined the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing as a judge, replacing Darcey Bussell, and she remains on its judging panel for the 2026 series while running a dance school in Germany.

name: Matthew Henson
aliases: Matthew Alexander Henson; Matthew A. Henson
description: Matthew Alexander Henson, born in Maryland in 1866, was the Arctic explorer who accompanied Robert E. Peary on the expeditions that claimed the North Pole on April 6, 1909. Orphaned as a boy, he went to work on a sailing ship at about thirteen, where the ship's skipper taught him to read and write. In 1887, working as a store clerk in Washington, D.C., he was hired by naval officer Robert Peary, then preparing an expedition to Nicaragua. Henson became Peary's most trusted expedition member: a navigator and craftsman who learned the Inuit language and survival skills, accompanied Peary on repeated Arctic expeditions, and, by his own account, arrived at the party's North Pole camp forty-five minutes ahead of Peary in 1909. Peary received most of the credit at the time, a slight Britannica attributes in part to racial prejudice against Henson as an African American. Henson told his own story in his 1912 book A Negro Explorer at the North Pole. He died in New York City on March 9, 1955. In 1988 he was reburied at Arlington National Cemetery beside Peary, and in 2000 the National Geographic Society awarded him its Hubbard Medal posthumously.

name: Mule Suttles
description: George "Mule" Suttles was a slugging first baseman and outfielder whose Negro leagues career ran from 1921 to 1944, spanning almost the entire golden era of segregated Black baseball. Born March 31, 1901, he emerged from Alabama coal country, where he had worked in the mines as a teenager, and joined the Birmingham Black Barons in 1923. He starred for the St. Louis Stars, helping them to Negro National League titles, and later played for the Chicago American Giants and the Newark Eagles, where he formed a celebrated infield alongside Willie Wells and Ray Dandridge. A right-handed hitter noted for tape-measure home runs, he topped .300 in twelve full seasons and was selected to five East-West Classic All-Star Games, hitting the first home run in that event in 1933 and a game-winning three-run homer in 1935. Fans greeted his at-bats with chants recorded by SABR. He managed the Newark Eagles in 1943 and 1944 and mentored younger players. Suttles died July 9, 1966, in Newark, New Jersey, and was posthumously inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 2006.

name: Michael Kutza
description: Michael Kutza is the Chicago graphic designer, filmmaker and film critic who founded the Chicago International Film Festival in 1964, at age 22, with the support of silent-screen star Colleen Moore; his memoir's account adds the help of director King Vidor. The festival debuted on November 9, 1965, at the Carnegie Theatre at Rush and Oak Streets, and Kutza then ran it for more than five decades: artistic director through 2017 — a tenure Cinema/Chicago identifies as longer than any other festival artistic director's — then chief executive of Cinema/Chicago, the presenting nonprofit he also founded, until his retirement at the end of 2018. Under Kutza the festival championed early work by Martin Scorsese (whose first feature it premiered in 1967), Rainer Werner Fassbinder, Wim Wenders, Claude Lelouch, Mike Leigh and Michael Moore, and hosted guests from Harold Lloyd and Bette Davis to Spike Lee, Halle Berry and Chadwick Boseman. He is the author of the memoir Starstruck: How I Magically Transformed Chicago into Hollywood for More Than Fifty Years, remains CEO Emeritus of Cinema/Chicago, and personally selects the festival's Founder's Award.

name: Makunde Martin
description: Makunde Martin is a co-founder of Chi Tech Collective, the Chicago community designed by and for Black technologists that addresses South Side disinvestment through education, mentorship, networking and pathways to tech employment and funding; 1871 also describes him as a software engineer at Google and a Campus 1871 speaker. He was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.

name: Malik Jackson
description: Malik Jackson is the publisher of the Chicago Reader, the nationally recognized alternative weekly founded in 1971 and known for community-centered journalism, investigative reporting and extensive local arts coverage; he took the role on June 1 under owner Noisy Creek, after serving as executive director and publisher of South Side Media Works, which operates South Side Weekly and the Hyde Park Herald. A third-generation Chicagoan who studied urban planning, he is not the NFL defensive lineman of the same name. He was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.

name: Malik Zambezi
description: Malik Zambezi is a Chicago-based documentary and street photographer working as 'Malik Shot You,' photographing people and places in Chicago communities not often represented. The Citizen Newspaper Group profiled his photography art walks through Chicago neighborhoods, the first running in Bronzeville from Metcalfe Park to Shawn Michelle's on 47th Street in October 2025. He was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.
